lines.text: A forty-five-year-old man presents with loin pain and haematuria. He has a palpable mass in his loin. What is the likely diagnosis?
The answer is renal cell carcinoma.
Three little friends make the classic triad. Haematuria, flank pain, and a loin mass.
The sick kidney pours red urine into a glass. That is haematuria.
The little kidney clutches its side. That is flank pain.
And on the big kidney, a tumour you can feel as a loin mass.
Renal cell carcinoma is also known as hypernephroma, Grawitz tumour, or clear cell carcinoma.
The complete triad is seen in only ten to fifteen per cent of patients.
Remember: haematuria, flank pain, and a loin mass mean renal cell carcinoma.

A sixty-eight-year-old man has acute painless frank haematuria. He had a similar episode several months ago, and has now noticed clots in his urine. His abdomen is soft and non-tender. What is the likely diagnosis?
The answer is transitional cell carcinoma.
This sixty-eight-year-old man passes frank red urine, and it is painless.
The bladder is full of frank blood. Painless haematuria is the key clue.
Lately he has noticed clots in his urine.
And the calendar remembers a similar episode several months ago.
Transitional epithelium lines the entire urinary tract, from the renal pelvis to the urethra.
Transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder is the most common cause of painless haematuria.
Remember: painless frank haematuria means transitional cell carcinoma until proven otherwise.
Select the best pairing of wound classification with the description.
The answer: a forty-two-year-old woman underwent an open cholecystectomy. The wound is clean contaminated, Class two.
A forty-two-year-old woman has an open cholecystectomy. The gallbladder is lifted out.
The wound opens the abdomen, and the surgeon breaches a hollow viscus.
(laugh) The little door is the hollow viscus, and the sign says it is not the colon.
Incisions that breach a hollow viscus other than the colon are clean contaminated wounds.
The infection rate is below ten per cent.
The Wound Judge stamps it: Class two.
Remember: open cholecystectomy is a clean contaminated wound, Class two.
